clue.text: Subterranean excavation, early Roman.

parts.note: an underground burial gallery of the kind dug by the first Christians of Rome

explanation.surface: A description of an archaeological dig beneath ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The early Christians of Rome buried their dead in underground tunnels, the best-known example of such galleries.

clue.text: 'Cutest non-Gothic' could be the up.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: "'Cutest non-Gothic' could be the up." The anagram of CUTEST NON GOTHIC is clear, but the definition is cut short ('the up.'), and neither a scan nor a search gives the rest.

clue.text: Be lofty!

parts.note: an order to stand very high above everything around, as a tall building or a tall person does

explanation.definitionFit: To rise high above one's surroundings is the verb's sense, a plain synonym for standing tall.

clue.text: Passionate-no doubt of that.

parts.note: describes someone quick-tempered and hot-headed, with a hint at the disease whose name is inside the word

explanation.surface: An emphatic remark about someone's fiery temperament.
explanation.walkthrough: The old humour 'choler' (yellow bile) was thought to make a person hot-tempered; the 'no doubt' teases that the word contains the name of a disease.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot-tempered, irascible person is easily roused to passion, the old medical sense of an excess of yellow bile.

clue.text: A help in conjuring things up.

definitions.text: A help in conjuring things up.

parts.words: A help in conjuring things up.
parts.note: conjuring up things here means a sorcerer or stage conjuror producing them out of nothing

explanation.surface: Something useful when you need to produce ideas from nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorcery or stage trickery is what lets a conjuror make things appear, so it is a help to him.

clue.text: Pre-bus turn-out-really grand!

indicators.note: the letters of the word are turned out and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Seeing the crowd before the bus leaves, someone declares the turnout splendid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn-out' looks like the noun for a crowd, but it signals that PREBUS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something magnificent or excellent is called splendid or grand, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Like some knotty thing at last resolved.

definitions.text: Like some knotty thing at last resolved.

parts.words: Like some knotty thing at last resolved.
parts.note: a knot that has finally been worked loose, or a knotty problem finally solved

explanation.surface: A tricky problem has finally been worked out.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot that has been untied is described as no longer fastened, the past participle of the verb to undo.

clue.text: Obviously not hopeless

parts.note: someone full of hope, and also a woman expecting a baby, plainly not without hope

explanation.definitionFit: Waiting hopefully for something to happen is the adjective's sense; it also describes a pregnant woman.

clue.text: One way to read, but seems dangerous place.

definitions.meaning: to find a hidden meaning in a text that is not stated outright
the ground between two opposing armies' trenches, an exposed and risky spot

explanation.definitionFit: Finding an implied meaning is an idiom for reading; and no man's land lies between the battle lines, a perilous place.

clue.text: Begin lessons without the boys-it's most surprising

parts.note: to begin is to start

indicators.note: lessons is written out with the boys left out of it

parts.note: boys are sons

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster finds that starting class with the boys absent is a great surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes SONS out of LESSONS, leaving LES.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that startles a person is very surprising, so 'it's most surprising' stands for the verb.

clue.text: 6 dn, in effect, with a hooligan inside.

definitions.text: 6 dn, in effect, with a hooligan inside.

parts.words: 6 dn, in effect, with a hooligan inside.
parts.note: the clue gives a word meaning not yet worked, near enough to 6 down's sense of left unfinished, and points to a rough type sitting inside that word

explanation.surface: A loosened knot with a lout caught in the middle of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 down is UNDONE. The clue offers a synonym in effect and then notes that a ROUGH (a hooligan) sits inside the answer; letters outside it are not separately clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal or work not yet shaped or worked is left undone in effect, so the adjective is a near synonym.

clue.text: Kind of store kept by some potter.

definitions.text: Kind of store kept by some potter.

parts.words: Kind of store kept by some potter.
parts.note: a storehouse or warehouse, with a play on pots being kept there by a potter

explanation.surface: A craftsman keeps his stock of wares in a storehouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the word ends in POT, the thing a potter makes; read as hidden in 'some potter', the letters fail, since there is no D.
explanation.definitionFit: A storehouse or warehouse for goods or military supplies is the word's sense, so a kind of store.

clue.text: "You are not like Cerberus, at once, are you ?" (Sheridan)

definitions.text: "You are not like Cerberus, at once, are you ?" (Sheridan)

parts.words: "You are not like Cerberus, at once, are you ?" (Sheridan)
parts.note: a line from Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's play The Rivals with a number left out: Cerberus, the guard dog of Hades, had that many heads

explanation.surface: A quotation from Sheridan's The Rivals with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop says no one can be Cerberus, 'three gentlemen at once'; the solver supplies the missing word, the dog's number of heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerberus in Greek myth had a trio of heads, so being like him means being that many people at once.

clue.text: "To suckle fools and" (Othello)

parts.note: the start of Iago's line in Othello, which goes on to a verb for recording trifles ('small beer')

explanation.surface: An incomplete quotation from Shakespeare's Othello.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago says a deserving woman is fit 'To suckle fools and chronicle small beer'; the solver supplies the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a verb meaning to record events in order, the next word of Iago's line.

clue.text: Surely not worth the examination?

parts.note: describes something so small or unimportant that it hardly bears looking at

explanation.surface: A doubtful question about whether something deserves scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Something too slight to matter is not worth considering, the adjective's plain sense.

clue.text: Fellows, possibly, able to make guards eat.

indicators.note: the letters of the two words can be made into something else, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A remark about men who can turn sentries into diners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'able to make' signals that GUARDSEAT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: College fellows have usually taken degrees, so they are an example of people holding a degree, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Unlike one of those city gents.

definitions.text: Unlike one of those city gents.

parts.words: Unlike one of those city gents.
parts.note: the polished city gentleman is suave and courteous; this is the opposite, with a play on a city being urban

explanation.surface: A remark that someone is nothing like a smart City businessman.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking polish or courtesy is the opposite of suave, which city gents are supposed to be; the word also plays on 'urban'.

clue.text: But the episcopal material isn't green.

definitions.text: But the episcopal material isn't green.

parts.words: But the episcopal material isn't green.
parts.note: the fine linen of a bishop's sleeves shares its name with a stretch of grass, but this sense is not the green one

explanation.surface: A remark that a bishop's vestments are not coloured green.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means fine linen, used for the sleeves of Anglican bishops' robes, and also a mown grass area; the clue picks the cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine linen or cambric is worn in Anglican bishops' sleeves, so it is episcopal material.

clue.text: We refill, maybe, but the choice is yours!

indicators.note: suggests the letters of the words could be in another arrangement

explanation.surface: A host topping up drinks tells guests they may decide for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The power of choosing for oneself, unconstrained, is the philosophical idea meant by 'the choice is yours'.

clue.text: The hoped-for end of an icy look.

definitions.text: The hoped-for end of an icy look.

parts.words: The hoped-for end of an icy look.
parts.note: a melting of frost, and also a warming of cold relations between people

explanation.surface: Someone hopes a frosty glance will soon soften.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice melting is the literal sense, and a relaxing of hostility is the figurative one, as with a cold stare.

clue.text: Win the rackers'championship?

parts.note: a contest among torturers who stretch victims on the rack, the winner being the one who stretches most

explanation.surface: A question about winning a contest among torturers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word normally means extend, but read as out- plus a verb it means beat others at stretching, which is what a racker does.
explanation.definitionFit: Out- prefixed to a verb means beat at it, so to stretch more than rivals would win such a contest.

clue.text: Footing of, for example, a driver

definitions.text: Footing of, for example, a driver

parts.words: Footing of, for example, a driver
parts.note: the position of the feet adopted by a golfer driving the ball off the tee

explanation.surface: A question about where a motorist puts their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driver' suggests a motorist, but it is a golfer using a driver club.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's position of the feet when addressing the ball is the sporting sense, so footing.

clue.text: Fair enough!

parts.note: describes something just and even-handed, read as a description rather than an expression of agreement

explanation.definitionFit: Being just and impartial is the meaning of fair, and the word means just that.

clue.text: It's usually doubled when posting.

parts.note: in bookkeeping, posting a transaction to the ledger records it twice, as debit and credit

explanation.surface: A remark about doubling something when sending a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'posting' suggests the mail, but it is the accountant's word for transferring items to a ledger, done by double-entry bookkeeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Each item recorded in a ledger is an item written in, and the double-entry system records it twice.

clue.text: What one may do at an 11 ac.

definitions.text: What one may do at an 11 ac.

parts.words: What one may do at an 11 ac.
parts.note: 11 across is a military base or storehouse where recruits sign up

explanation.surface: A question about what to do at a storehouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is DEPOT, also a regimental base where new soldiers register.
explanation.definitionFit: Signing up as a member or recruit is the verb's sense, which recruits do at a regimental base.

clue.text: Such incursions must have inside assistance.

definitions.text: Such incursions must have inside assistance.

parts.words: Such incursions must have inside assistance.
parts.note: attacks of this kind contain a word for help in their middle, and burglaries often have an accomplice within

explanation.surface: A claim that break-ins always need help from someone on the inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The word has AID (assistance) inside it, a hint rather than full wordplay, since the outer R and S are not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden attacks or forays into enemy territory are incursions, so the plural matches.

clue.text: Yet five is always half this

definitions.text: Yet five is always half this

parts.words: Yet five is always half this
parts.note: five is half of the number after nine, and the word for frequently, read as two words, says exactly that

explanation.surface: A paradoxical remark about the number five.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as OF TEN, it completes 'five is half of ten'; whole, it means frequently, picking up 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: Frequently, many times, is the adverb's sense, close to the clue's 'always'.

clue.text: "Fix'd like a plant. propagate and rot." (Pope)

definitions.text: "Fix'd like a plant. propagate and rot." (Pope)

parts.words: "Fix'd like a plant. propagate and rot." (Pope)
parts.note: lines from Pope's Essay on Man with words left out: a plant on its spot is there 'to draw' its food from the soil

explanation.surface: An abridged couplet from Pope's Essay on Man.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope wrote 'Fix'd like a plant on his peculiar spot, To draw nutrition, propagate, and rot'; the solver supplies the missing noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Nourishment drawn from food or soil is the missing noun's sense, what a rooted plant draws.

clue.text: No tailor this to give you a gore.

definitions.text: No tailor this to give you a gore.

parts.words: No tailor this to give you a gore.
parts.note: a gore is a tapering panel a tailor sews in, but also a wound from a horn or tusk

explanation.surface: A warning that this is not the dressmaker who will add a panel to your skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: A tailor's gore is a triangular piece of cloth; to gore is also to pierce with a tusk, as an elephant or boar does.
explanation.definitionFit: An elephant or wild boar with well-grown tusks is so called, and such a beast can gore.
